issues.legal_issue: An agreement for sale that requires the vendor to obtain statutory permission before completing the sale is not barred from specific performance merely because the land is subject to a ceiling restriction.
material_facts: The agreement placed on the vendors the obligation to obtain permission from the competent authority before completing the sale.
The vendors did not obtain that permission and were found to be in breach of the agreement.
The property was part of a larger holding, and the vendors could have retained the property within their applicable ceiling limit by obtaining permission.
The agreement did not require an unlawful transfer without permission.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was not void from its inception, and the contractual obligation to obtain permission could be enforced. The earlier Full Bench ruling did not prevent specific performance on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: The Full Bench ruling between the parties was binding, including on issues of law arising from the same cause of action (Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v. Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy). But that ruling distinguished agreements requiring the vendor to obtain permission from agreements for an unlawful transfer of excess land, and recognised that a decree cannot impose a condition that departs from the contract. The Court applied that distinction to the agreement’s express permission clause. It also relied on Sushila v. Nihalchand Nahata for the understanding that agreements concerning land to be exempted or otherwise lawfully transferred can be enforceable.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit_on_appeal and agreement_requires_vendor_permission and vendor_failed_to_obtain_permission and transfer_not_contracted_without_permission

predicates.specific_performance_suit_on_appeal: A purchaser brought a suit for specific performance and the matter is before an appellate court.
predicates.agreement_requires_vendor_permission: The sale agreement makes the vendor responsible for obtaining required permission before completing the sale.
predicates.vendor_failed_to_obtain_permission: The vendor did not obtain the required permission.
predicates.transfer_not_contracted_without_permissi: The agreement does not require the parties to complete a transfer in a manner that disregards the required permission.

issues.definition: When an appellate court considers a specific-performance suit involving an agreement that assigns the vendor the task of obtaining permission, it may enforce the agreement if the vendor failed to obtain permission and the agreement does not require an unpermitted transfer.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory repeal occurring while an appeal is pending may remove a statutory impediment to specific performance when the repeal applies to the pending proceeding and no relevant vested right or saved transaction prevents its application.
material_facts: The suit remained pending on appeal when the urban land ceiling law was repealed.
No steps had been taken under the repealed law to vest the land in the State or take possession of it.
The repeal’s savings provisions covered specified completed or protected matters, none of which applied to the property.
The vendors had no vested right under the repealed law that was affected by applying the repeal in the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The repealed law did not prevent a decree for specific performance when the appellate decree was made.
issues.legal_principle: An appeal is a continuation and rehearing of the suit, and a change in law during an appeal may govern the parties’ rights unless it takes away a vested right. The Court relied on Rameshwar v. Jot Ram, Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, Dayawati v. Inderjit, Amarjit Kaur v. Pritam Singh, and Lakshmi Narayan Guin v. Niranjan Modak. It applied the repeal and savings provisions and relied on Gajraj Singh v. State Transport Appellate Tribunal and India Tobacco Co. Ltd. v. CTO on the effect of repeal. It distinguished Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay because no fundamental or vested right of the vendors was affected.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit_on_appeal and law_repealed_while_appeal_pending and no_saved_vesting_or_possession and no_vested_defendant_right

predicates.specific_performance_suit_on_appeal: A specific-performance suit is still being decided in an appeal when the relevant law changes.
predicates.law_repealed_while_appeal_pending: The law that created the asserted impediment was repealed while the appeal remained pending.
predicates.no_saved_vesting_or_possession: The property was not within a completed vesting or possession situation preserved by the repeal’s savings provisions.
predicates.no_vested_defendant_right: Applying the repeal does not take away a vested right held by the defendant.

issues.definition: If a law creating an impediment is repealed during an appeal, the repeal may govern the pending specific-performance suit where no saved completed action or vested defendant right prevents that result.

issues.legal_issue: Delay caused by the court process, without more, does not justify denying specific performance to a purchaser who was ready and willing to perform and whose suit was filed within limitation.
material_facts: The purchaser pleaded readiness and willingness and deposited the balance consideration in court.
The purchaser filed suit after the vendors failed to complete their contractual obligations.
The findings that the vendors were in breach and the purchaser remained ready and willing were not displaced.
The lengthy passage of time before the appellate decision resulted from the court process, not from default by the purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The delay in the court process could not be held against the purchaser to deny specific performance. The Court restored the decree for specific performance and required the purchaser to pay an additional amount offered during the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as it stood before amendment, discretion to grant specific performance had to be exercised on sound judicial principles; delay caused by the court process was not by itself a ground to refuse relief. Mere delay or escalation in property prices is not alone sufficient. The Court relied on Mademsetty Satyanarayana v. G. Yelloji Rao, Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd., P. D’Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu, P.S. Ramaswamy Reddy v. M.K. Bhagyalakshmi, Narinderjit Singh v. North Star Estate Promoters Ltd., Satya Jain v. Anis Ahmed Rushdie, and other cases addressing delay, price escalation, and equitable conditions. It distinguished cases involving purchaser default, including K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan and Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit_on_appeal and suit_within_limitation and purchaser_ready_and_willing and vendor_breach and delay_caused_by_court_process

predicates.specific_performance_suit_on_appeal: A suit for specific performance is before an appellate court.
predicates.suit_within_limitation: The purchaser brought the suit within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.purchaser_ready_and_willing: The purchaser remained ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s contractual obligations.
predicates.vendor_breach: The vendor failed to perform an obligation required by the sale agreement.
predicates.delay_caused_by_court_process: The time taken to resolve the case resulted from the court process rather than the purchaser’s default.

issues.definition: A purchaser who sued within limitation and remained ready and willing to perform is not denied specific performance solely because the court process delayed the decision after the vendor’s breach.
